title: ACSM Resistance Training Prescription Position Stand
scope: Healthy adults; general resistance training outcomes, not boxing-specific programming.
summary: Strength is generally supported by heavier loads, full range of motion, multiple sets and regular practice. Power work commonly uses moderate loads with low-to-moderate volume.
limitations: Population-level guidance; it does not prescribe an individualized weekly plan or medical care.

title: Resistance training dose-response meta-regression
scope: Resistance training volume and frequency across study populations.
summary: Higher volume and frequency can support strength gains with diminishing returns; frequency is partly a way to distribute volume and movement practice.
limitations: Does not define the best schedule for one boxer and should not justify adding days without recovery data.

title: Proximity to failure and resistance training adaptations
scope: Resistance training proximity to failure, strength and hypertrophy.
summary: Strength improvements occur across a broad range of repetitions in reserve; training every set to failure is not required.
limitations: The exact dose-response remains uncertain; a fixed RIR target is still a configurable heuristic.

title: Autoregulated resistance training for maximal strength enhancement
scope: APRE, RPE and velocity-based approaches for maximal strength.
summary: Autoregulated approaches can be effective for maximal strength and may outperform fixed percentage-based loading in some comparisons.
limitations: Published protocols do not validate this bot's exact 2.5-5 percent adjustment rules.

title: RIR-based RPE scale for resistance training
scope: Resistance-trained squatters and perceived repetitions in reserve.
summary: RPE anchored to repetitions in reserve is a practical way to communicate effort during resistance exercise.
limitations: RIR accuracy varies by person, exercise and experience and should be calibrated over time.

title: Monitoring athlete training response using subjective measures
scope: Subjective and objective monitoring of athlete response to training load.
summary: Subjective wellbeing measures can be sensitive and useful for tracking changes within an athlete.
limitations: Subjective fatigue or soreness is context, not a standalone diagnosis of overtraining.

title: Compatibility of concurrent aerobic and strength training
scope: Concurrent aerobic and strength training; not specifically contact boxing or sparring.
summary: Concurrent training does not necessarily impair maximal strength or hypertrophy, while explosive strength can be more sensitive to interference and scheduling.
limitations: Boxing combines skill, intervals and contact; direct boxing-specific conclusions are an extrapolation.

title: Effects of rest interval duration in resistance training
scope: Rest intervals and chronic strength development.
summary: Longer rest intervals, often above two minutes, can better support maximal strength in trained individuals.
limitations: Rest should still reflect exercise, load, time constraints and the athlete's response.

title: PAR-Q+ official pre-participation screening pathway
scope: Pre-participation screening and referral pathway.
summary: The official pathway helps determine whether further exercise-professional or healthcare review is appropriate before increasing physical activity.
limitations: Do not copy, alter or embed the protected questionnaire without permission; link to the official current version.

title: Effects of resistance training performed to repetition failure or non-failure
scope: Resistance training to failure versus non-failure for strength and hypertrophy.
summary: Training to momentary failure is not required for strength development when training volume is considered.
limitations: This does not define one ideal reserve target for every exercise, athlete or phase.

title: Effects of combined upper- and lower-limb plyometric training
scope: Healthy participants performing combined upper- and lower-body plyometric training.
summary: Plyometric training can improve power-related performance, speed and strength; explosive work should emphasize high-quality repetitions rather than fatigue.
limitations: Exercise choice and dose still need to match experience, equipment, sport load and joint tolerance.

title: Effects of velocity loss in strength training
scope: Velocity-loss thresholds during resistance training in trained rowers.
summary: Limiting within-set velocity loss can preserve movement quality and support strength development with less fatigue than training to failure.
limitations: Without a velocity sensor, visible slowing is only a practical proxy and should not be presented as measured power.

title: Accuracy of repetitions-in-reserve estimation
scope: Perceived repetitions remaining across different resistance-training loads.
summary: Reserve estimates are a useful subjective autoregulation signal but tend to be more accurate with heavier than lighter loads.
limitations: Treat the estimate as one input alongside completed work, technique, pain and perceived difficulty, not as objective truth.

title: Resistance training load effects on muscle hypertrophy and strength gain
scope: Low, moderate and high resistance-training loads with volume load equated.
summary: Higher loads favor gains in one-repetition maximum strength, while hypertrophy can be similar across a wider range of loads when training volume is matched.
limitations: This does not establish a universal maximum number of sets or make one light set equivalent to one heavy set.

title: Monitoring exercise load in resistance training
scope: Methods for describing and monitoring resistance-training dose.
summary: Resistance-training dose depends on several interacting variables, including load, volume, repetitions, rest and movement velocity; no single measure fully describes it.
limitations: Tonnage and raw set count are useful descriptors but cannot by themselves quantify fatigue or training stimulus.

title: Influence of resistance exercise order on strength and hypertrophy
scope: Exercise order in resistance-training sessions and its effect on strength and hypertrophy.
summary: Strength gains tend to be greatest for exercises performed near the beginning of a session, supporting placement of the priority lift first.
limitations: Exercise order evidence does not create a universal prohibition on combining particular lifts in one session.

title: Influence of proximity to failure, relative intensity, and volume on fatigue after resistance training
scope: Acute voluntary-performance, neuromuscular and perceived fatigue after resistance training.
summary: Set duration, proximity to failure, total volume and training density are important fatigue determinants, so a session must be evaluated as a combined dose.
limitations: The literature does not provide one validated session-fatigue score or a fixed list of exercise combinations that must be banned.

title: Recovery after squat, bench press and deadlift
scope: Recovery after four sets to failure at 80% 1RM in twelve well-trained men.
summary: Recovery and muscle-damage responses were broadly similar across squat, bench press and deadlift; deadlift was not uniquely more damaging.
limitations: Small male sample and one failure-based protocol; this does not make all exercises or doses equally fatiguing.

title: Strength training in Olympic combat sports athletes
scope: Strength-training interventions in judo, boxing, karate, wrestling and fencing athletes.
summary: Appropriately programmed strength training improved strength, power and some sport-specific outcomes in Olympic combat athletes.
limitations: Interventions and sports were heterogeneous; the review does not identify a universal best exercise list for boxing.

title: Resistance training and range of motion
scope: Chronic resistance training and joint range of motion in healthy participants.
summary: Resistance training with external loads improved range of motion and was not inferior to stretching for that outcome.
limitations: Results do not mean every partial-range program preserves every boxing-specific mobility requirement.

title: Resistance exercise and muscle stiffness
scope: Acute and chronic changes in ultrasound-measured muscle stiffness after resistance exercise.
summary: Muscle stiffness rose briefly after a session but was not increased by long-term resistance training in the available studies.
limitations: Few studies were available and ultrasound stiffness is not the same as boxing movement quality.

title: Recovery from resistance exercise with different set configurations
scope: Bench press and squat protocols differing in repetitions completed relative to possible repetitions.
summary: Sets taken to failure, especially at higher repetitions, produced greater fatigue and slower neuromuscular recovery.
limitations: This does not define one reserve target for every athlete, lift or training phase.
